## How old is origami?

Ask almost anyone and you get the same answer: an ancient Japanese art, a thousand years old or more, handed down from the Heian court. I believed it too, and repeated it, until I went looking for the evidence. There is almost none. What survives tells a shorter and more interesting story: folding grew in two places that knew nothing of each other, Japan and Europe, for different reasons, and the thing we call origami is a product of their meeting in the late nineteenth century and a creative explosion in the twentieth. The oldest firmly dated picture of a paper crane is from 1591, and we have known that only since 2017.

Here is the story as the documents tell it, with the dates that can be defended.

## Paper first

Nothing can be folded before it exists. Chinese tradition credits paper to the court official Cai Lun in 105 CE, but archaeology has pushed the material itself back: fragments found at Fangmatan in Gansu date from the second century BCE. Cai Lun's contribution was the process, cheap and repeatable, using bark, hemp and rags. From China the craft moved to Korea and, according to the *Nihon Shoki*, reached Japan in 610 through the monk Donchō. Whether Donchō introduced papermaking or was merely good at it, the Japanese took the craft further than anyone: *washi*, made from the long fibres of the paper mulberry, is strong enough to be folded and refolded, and that property matters for everything that follows.

[Unknown pre-modern painter](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Making_Paper.gif), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.](images/papermaking-1637.png){fig-alt="Five woodcut panels showing the stages of traditional Chinese papermaking, from soaking the bark and fibres to drying the sheets" fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Japan: folding before play

The first Japanese folds were not toys. Paper was expensive and sacred. At Shinto shrines the zigzag *shide* streamers and *gohei* wands are folded paper, and they are old. From the Heian period (794–1185) we have *tatō*, folded paper packets carried by gentlemen, and codes for folding letters. In the Muromachi period (1333–1573) the samurai households of Ise and Ogasawara wrote down the etiquette of *tsutsumi*, the formal wrapping of gifts, and the *noshi* ornament attached to them. The paired butterflies *ochō* and *mechō* that dress sake flasks at weddings belong to this ceremonial tradition; the earliest drawing of them is in the *Onna Chōhōki* of 1692, and Ise Sadatake's *Tsutsumi-no-ki* of 1764 describes thirteen ceremonial folds.

This is *girei origami*, ceremonial folding: abstract, stylised, governed by rules. It is not what we mean by origami today, but it kept the habit of folding alive among people who had paper to spare, and the butterflies are the one ceremonial design that looks like a model.

## The first crane

For a long time the standard account, which I repeated in an earlier version of this essay, held that there was no evidence of folding for pleasure in Japan before about 1600, and the first dated pictures came from the 1700s. That changed in 2017. A *kozuka*, the small knife handle fitted to a sword scabbard, made by the metalworker Gotō Eijō (1577–1617), turned out to be decorated with three paper cranes beside a pine tree. The piece has since been dated to 1591–93. It is a tiny object, 9.7 cm long and 1.4 cm wide, and it moves the paper crane, one of the most refined of the traditional folds, back a full century.

![An origami crane on an *inrō*, a lacquered case for small items that hung from the sash.. Photo: Jōka, [CC BY-SA 2.0 FR](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/fr/deed.en), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Origami_Crane_inro-Ethno_BHM_1070-P8260166.JPG).](images/inro-crane.jpg){fig-alt="A black lacquered inrō hanging from a brown silk cord, with a silver-grey origami crane and a gold bamboo-like plant in relief on its front" fig-align="center" width="45%"}

Who owned such an object matters. The Gotō family made sword fittings for shoguns and warlords, and only a general, a lord or someone close to them could possess a Gotō piece; Eijō himself served Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Koshiro Hatori, in the 2017 study that made the kozuka known to the origami world, draws the conclusion that folding for pleasure already existed in samurai society, before it reached the townspeople of the Edo period. Ceremonial and recreational folding, he suggests, were not yet two separate things, and passed to the towns together. On his reading, the century between the kozuka and the first pattern books is not a hole in the evidence: it is the time the habit took to cross from the samurai class into town culture.

The object also has a puzzle of its own. The central crane is carved accurately, but the two outer ones have an odd shape, like a hooded warrior with a hump behind. Hatori tried to fold that shape and could not reproduce it with simple folds. Eijō was a master engraver, so clumsiness is unlikely; Hatori's guess is that neither he nor the people around him knew how to fold a crane, and that he carved the sides from imagination, working from a front view alone. If so, the crane was still new, and little known even among samurai, in the 1590s. And why an *origami* crane rather than a real one? Okamura Masao, an adviser to the Nippon Origami Association, has offered a hypothesis. Hideyoshi's long-awaited heir, Tsurumatsu ("Crane Pine"), died at the age of two in the summer of 1591. A real crane is an auspicious bird and would have been wrong for a memorial piece, and the pine, in this case, would be a young one. It is a conjecture, not a fact, but it is the kind of question we can ask only because the object survived.

One crane proves little about how many other folds existed; it is simply the one that happened to be engraved on something that has survived. After it, the record thickens quickly:

- 1680: Ihara Saikaku's verse about folded butterflies, possibly the *ochō* and *mechō*.
- 1700–1713: cranes, a treasure ship and a boat appear as motifs in kimono pattern books.
- 1717: a print, *Keisei ori tsuru*, shows a child learning to fold in a temple school, with a crane and a *komosō* (a monk in a basket hat) beside her.
- 1734: *Ranma zushiki*, a book of patterns for carved transoms, shows a boat, a *komosō*, a thread container, a *sanbō* offering tray and a *tamatebako* box, the earliest modular design.
- 1797: *Hiden senbazuru orikata*, the first printed book devoted to folding, by Akisato Ritō: 49 ways to fold linked cranes from a single slit sheet.
- 1845: the *Kan no mado* manuscript of Adachi Kazuyuki, 48 designs including the frog, the cicada and the iris, which lay unpublished until 1961.

By the Edo period, then, folding for fun was ordinary: *orikata*, *orisue*, *orimono*, several words for it, none of them yet "origami" in our sense.

![Page from the *Hiden Senbazuru Orikata* ("The Secret of One Thousand Cranes Origami"), 1797. [Unknown monk from Japan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hiden_Senbazuru_Orikata-S8-1.jpg), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.](images/senbazuru-1797.jpg){fig-alt="Woodblock-printed page showing linked paper cranes titled Inazuma (lightning) with a short poem, and the slit-cut diagram of the sheet at the bottom" fig-align="center" width="45%"}

## Europe: napkins, puzzles and the cocotte

Europe got paper late, through the Arab world: Spain by the eleventh century, Italy by the thirteenth. And it folded other things first. Fifteenth-century Italian banquets were decorated with linen folded into animals, castles and fountains; Mattia Giegher, who taught the subject in Padua, published the first treatise on the "art of folding" in 1629, and his designs crossed into Germany with Harsdörffer's *Trincir-Buch*. Several napkin forms, the waterbomb base among them, reappear later in paper.

For paper itself, the earliest firm evidence is unglamorous: a box, shown being folded in the illustrated *Hours of Catherine of Cleves* around 1440. Luca Pacioli's puzzle manuscript of about 1500 contains folded-paper tricks. The small paper boat often cited from a 1498 edition of Sacrobosco's *Sphaera* is doubtful, and the "paper prisons" for flies in Webster's *Duchess of Malfi* may or may not be the waterbomb; honest histories now mark both with a question mark.

Through the eighteenth century, European folding was a matter of toys and parlour tricks: paper hats, bangers, the "troublewit" pleated sheet, card castles. Then a bird. The *cocotte*, a little hen folded from a square, appears in a French painting of 1801 and gets its first written instructions in 1827. The Spanish call it the *pajarita* and claim it as their own; the Spanish evidence, from 1847, is later, and Miguel de Unamuno's *cocotología* of the 1900s, folding birds in Salamanca cafés, was a revival rather than a root.

## Fröbel and the kindergarten

The person who made folding a world practice was not a folder but a teacher. Friedrich Fröbel opened the first *Kindergarten* in 1840 and built its curriculum from "gifts" and "occupations", and paper folding was one of the occupations: Forms of Life (useful objects), Forms of Beauty (symmetrical patterns) and Forms of Knowledge (geometry: halves, diagonals, the square's relation to the triangle). He died in 1852, but the kindergartens multiplied, and wherever they went they carried packets of coloured squares and a set of standard folds.

They reached Japan in 1876, when the first kindergarten opened at the Tokyo Women's Normal School. Within a decade Japanese children were folding Fröbel's geometric patterns alongside the crane and the *komosō*, and the two traditions had merged in the classroom.

## The meeting

Traffic ran the other way too. Japan showed at the Paris Exposition of 1867, and Japanese folds, the crane and above all the flapping bird, turned up in European magazines and conjuring books from the 1880s. By the time *Origami zusetsu* (1908) formally separated ceremonial from recreational folding, the word *origami* was settling into its modern meaning, and the craft was already international, though nobody called it that yet.

## The modern era

Three people, in three countries, turned a children's craft into an art. In Japan, Akira Yoshizawa (1911–2005) spent the 1930s and 40s inventing: thousands of original models, the wet-folding technique that lets paper hold a curve, and in 1954 a notation of dotted lines and arrows that anyone could read. In the United States, Lillian Oppenheimer founded the Origami Center of New York in 1958 and, with Gershon Legman, who had organised the first Western exhibition of Yoshizawa's work in Amsterdam in 1955, connected folders across the world by letter. In Britain, Robert Harbin's *Paper Magic* (1956) and the founding of the British Origami Society (1967) did the same. When Samuel Randlett's *The Art of Origami* (1961) adopted Yoshizawa's symbols, the Yoshizawa–Randlett system became the common written language of the craft, and it still is.

## From art to mathematics

The last chapter is the one this site is about. Once there was a notation, people began to ask what folding *could* do, and the first answer came as a list.

In 1986 the French mathematician Jacques Justin published a set of seven elementary single-fold operations: each one asks for a crease that achieves one or more alignments between given points and lines on the sheet (Justin 1986). The paper appeared in a French journal for teachers and was largely overlooked. Humiaki Huzita rediscovered six of the operations and presented them at the first international meeting on origami science and technology, in Ferrara in 1989 (Huzita 1989). The seventh was found again by Koshiro Hatori in 2001, according to Alperin and Lang (2006). That is why the list goes by several names, Huzita's, Huzita–Justin or Huzita–Hatori axioms. Strictly they are operations rather than axioms in a logician's sense, but the name has stuck, and I use it on this site too.

What makes them important is what they can do. Taken together they are a stronger geometric toolkit than straightedge and compass: they solve cubic equations (Alperin 2000), and with them one can trisect an arbitrary angle (Hull 1996), double the cube, and construct the regular heptagon (Geretschläger 1997), none of which compass and straightedge can do.

Other results followed. Justin's name returns in the local conditions for a crease pattern to fold flat, the Maekawa–Justin and Kawasaki–Justin theorems. Robert Lang's *TreeMaker* (1990s) turned the design of an insect with the right number of legs into an optimisation problem. Koryo Miura's fold of 1970 went into a solar array. The international meetings on origami in science, mathematics and education, which began in Ferrara in 1989 and are now known as OSME, are where folders, mathematicians and engineers compare notes, and their proceedings are the field's record.

That is the real sense in which origami is ancient: not that the crane is a thousand years old, but that a square of paper has been a laboratory for geometry since the first person folded a corner to a corner and noticed what the crease did.

## Fold it yourself

Fold the crane, and as you do, notice that it is harder than it looks: a bird base with a double sink is a serious piece of engineering for 1591. Then fold the two butterflies, *ochō* and *mechō*; they are easier, older in spirit, and the asymmetry between male and female is a small lesson in how ceremonial folding encodes meaning.

## Classroom note

Level: 12 and up. Time: one period. Materials: a printed timeline and, for the last step, a square of paper per student.

This activity is about historical evidence, not folding. Give students these dated items from the story above: the cranes on the kozuka (a small decorated knife handle that fits on a sword scabbard, 1591–93), Saikaku's verse about butterflies (1680), the print of a child learning to fold (1717), *Ranma zushiki* (1734), *Hiden senbazuru orikata* (1797) and the *Kan no mado* manuscript (1845). Then ask three questions:

1. Which items show that people folded paper *for pleasure*, and which could be about ritual or something else? (The 1680 verse is a good one to argue over: the butterflies may be ceremonial.)
2. How do we know the date of each item? What would make you doubt it?
3. Until 2017, histories said there was no firm evidence of recreational folding in Japan before about 1600. One engraved sword fitting changed that. Why can a single dated object change the story, when a claim repeated a thousand times, such as "origami is a thousand years old", cannot?

To finish, students fold the [crane](https://web-japan.org/kidsweb/virtual/origami/exploring02f.html) and the [ochō](https://origami-resource-center.com/formal-ocho/)/[mechō](https://origami-resource-center.com/formal-mecho/) butterflies and decide which of the two they would expect to find in the oldest records, and why.
